nature-eecon-238.title: Energy: the quantity that is conserved and dissipated
nature-eecon-238.text:
Energy is conserved. The total energy of an isolated system stays constant, though it can change form. The first law of thermodynamics says the same of a closed system: its energy is constant unless transferred in or out as work or heat. Energy is the quantitative property transferred to a body or system, seen in the capacity to do work and in heat and light.

Its SI unit is the joule, the work done by one newton over one metre. Power, energy per unit time, is measured in watts, one joule per second. Total energy divides into potential and kinetic energy, and forms such as mechanical or nuclear energy are combinations of the two. In irreversible processes energy is dissipated into available states and cannot be recovered into more concentrated forms without degrading more energy.

Living things need an external source: sunlight for green plants, chemical energy for animals. Cellular respiration stores energy in carbohydrates, lipids and proteins. Sunlight is the main input to Earth's energy budget, which accounts for its temperature and climate stability.

nature-eecon-239.title: Renewable energy: power replenished on a human timescale
nature-eecon-239.text:
Renewable energy is made from natural resources replenished on a human timescale. The most widely used types are solar, wind, bioenergy and hydropower, and the IEA defines it as energy from natural processes replenished faster than they are consumed. Replacing fossil fuels with low-emission sources is central to net zero. Renewables are also more evenly spread worldwide than fossil fuels and cut air pollution.

The resource is vast. The technical potential of utility-scale solar PV, concentrated solar, onshore wind and offshore wind each exceeds 100 PWh per year, against global energy use of about 65 PWh in 2019. IRENA states that about 86% (187 GW) of renewable capacity added in 2022 cost less than fossil-fuel electricity, and its finance report shows US$499 billion invested that year. Investment in renewables, especially solar, tends to create more jobs than coal, gas or oil.

There are catches. Solar and wind are intermittent, with lower capacity factors, while fossil, nuclear and hydropower plants can match the grid's demand. Storage returns energy when production falls below consumption. Critics note that renewables need more metals and minerals whose extraction can cause environmental conflict, and installations increasingly threaten conservation areas. Whether nuclear power counts as renewable is debated; legal definitions usually exclude it, with Utah an exception.

nature-eecon-241.title: Money: what everyone agrees to accept
nature-eecon-241.text:
Money is any item or verifiable record generally accepted as payment for goods and services and repayment of debts in a given country or context. Its functions are medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value and sometimes standard of deferred payment. Jevons's 1875 four-function analysis became the couplet 'A Medium, a Measure, a Standard, a Store'.

Each function solves a problem. As a medium of exchange, money avoids barter's problem of ensuring a coincidence of wants. As a unit of account it lets prices be quoted, and it is a prerequisite for debt agreements and accounting systems. As a store of value it must be reliably storable and keep a stable value over time. It is the most liquid asset because it is universally accepted as a common currency.

Nearly all contemporary money is unbacked fiat money, valued by government order and social convention rather than intrinsic value. It is created in two ways. Central banks issue cash, called narrow money, and private banks create broad money by recording loans as deposits.

nature-eecon-240.title: Mathematical models: abstract descriptions of real systems
nature-eecon-240.text:
A mathematical model is an abstract description of a concrete system using mathematical concepts and language. It describes the system by variables and equations relating them, and is used to predict behaviour or solve specific problems. Models can be linear or nonlinear, static or dynamic (differential or difference equations), discrete or continuous, and deterministic or stochastic.

Their foundations differ. A deductive model rests on theory, an inductive model on empirical generalization, and a 'floating' model on neither. Strategic models used in game theory treat players as autonomous decision makers who rationally maximize an objective function.

Complexity trades simplicity against accuracy. By Occam's razor, among models of similar predictive power the simplest is preferred. Models are checked by splitting data into training data, which set the parameters, and verification data. Scope asks whether the model holds between data points (interpolation) or beyond them (extrapolation). Models with no a priori information are black boxes and those with all necessary information are white boxes; practically all systems lie between.

nature-eecon-244.title: Energy storage: moving power through time
nature-eecon-244.text:
Energy storage captures energy produced at one time so it can be used later, which reduces imbalances between demand and supply. In practice it means converting energy from forms that are hard to store into forms that are more convenient or cheaper to store. It helps overcome the intermittency of {{ref:nature-eecon-239}}.

Pumped-storage hydroelectricity is the largest-capacity form of active grid storage. EPRI reported in March 2012 that it accounts for over 99% of bulk storage capacity worldwide. Its efficiency varies in practice between 70% and 80%, with claims of up to 87%. Other families include compressed air, flywheels, thermal storage, rechargeable and flow batteries, supercapacitors, and chemical routes such as power-to-gas, turning electricity into hydrogen or methane.

Limits remain. To exceed 40% self-sufficiency in a household with photovoltaics, storage is needed. Cost makes batteries impractical for the large storage needed to balance seasonal swings. The economics depend on the reserve service requested and several uncertain factors, so the best storage size is market and location dependent.

nature-eecon-245.title: Green building: efficiency from planning to demolition
nature-eecon-245.text:
As of 2020 buildings account for 37% of global energy use and energy-related CO2 emissions; counting the manufacture of building materials, the share is 39%. UNEP warns that without new construction technologies emissions from buildings could double by 2050. Green building answers this. It is both a structure and the processes that make it environmentally responsible and resource-efficient across its life cycle, from planning to demolition.

Life cycle assessment covers all cradle-to-grave impacts, such as embodied energy, global warming potential, resource use, pollution and waste. It is the best way to evaluate buildings but is not yet a consistent requirement of rating systems. As buildings use less operating energy, embodied energy can reach as much as 30% of life cycle energy consumption.

Most green buildings cost a premium of under 2% but yield 10 times as much over the building's life. Even so, price is the most criticized issue, since photovoltaics, new appliances and modern technologies tend to cost more. Rating systems such as BREEAM (UK), LEED (US and Canada), DGNB (Germany), CASBEE (Japan) and GRIHA (India) help consumers judge a structure's environmental level.

nature-eecon-246.title: Post-Keynesian economics: demand without automatic full employment
nature-eecon-246.text: Post-Keynesian economics is a heterodox, non-equilibrium school that grew out of Keynes's General Theory and was developed by Kalecki, Robinson, Kaldor, Weintraub and others. Its foundation is effective demand: demand matters in the long run as well as the short run, so a market economy has no automatic tendency toward full employment. Unlike new Keynesians, post-Keynesians do not blame sticky prices or wages for that failure. They stress that money supply responds to bank credit demand, so a central bank can only manage the interest rate. Strands include Kalecki's class-based demand, Kaldor's increasing returns, Minsky's financial fragility and Modern Monetary Theory. Cambridge Econometrics built the E3ME model, which the European Commission uses to analyse its policies.

nature-eecon-242.title: Types of money, from shells to bank databases
nature-eecon-242.text: Money comes in several kinds: commodity, representative, fiat, demurrage, commercial bank and digital. Commodity money takes its value from what it is made of, such as precious metals, shells or barley. Representative money is tokens exchangeable for a fixed quantity of a commodity like gold or silver. Demurrage currency is designed to lose purchasing power at a constant rate, serving only as a temporary store of value, and differs in effect from inflation. By the 2000s most money existed as digital currency in bank databases.

nature-eecon-243.title: Deliberative democracy: legitimacy through real discussion
nature-eecon-243.text: Deliberative democracy puts deliberation at the center of decision-making and treats it as the source of legitimacy for law. A decision counts as legitimate only if authentic deliberation, free of the distortions of unequal political power, came first. Counting votes is not enough. James Fishkin names five characteristics of legitimate deliberation: information, substantive balance, diversity, conscientiousness and equal consideration. His trilemma holds that institutions can achieve only two of political equality, mass participation and deliberation. Mini-publics chosen by sortition deliberate on behalf of the public. The OECD documented hundreds of examples, with use increasing since 2010, and Ireland puts assembly recommendations to a national referendum.

nature-eecon-247.title: Urban metabolism: the city as a flow of materials
nature-eecon-247.text:
Abel Wolman coined the term in 1965 by modelling the inflows and outflows of a hypothetical American city of 1 million people, mainly water and the waste it produces. Urban metabolism is now a model for describing the flows of materials and energy through cities, as in a city-level material flow analysis.

Herbert Girardet contrasted circular metabolism, where nearly everything is reused, with the linear metabolism of cities, with clear resource inputs and waste outputs. Howard T. Odum's energy method coined emergy, which measures the solar energy used directly or indirectly to make a product, in solar equivalent joules. Material flow analysis became the mainstream school because its units are more practical for the public, officials and researchers. Planners use it for four things: sustainability reporting, urban greenhouse gas accounting, mathematical modelling for policy analysis and urban design.

nature-eecon-256.title: Robert Solow: growth from technical progress
nature-eecon-256.text:
Robert Solow is the American economist behind the Solow-Swan growth model, and he won the 1987 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences. His model separates the determinants of growth into increases in inputs (labour and capital) and technical progress. It is called exogenous because the saving rate is taken as given. Using it, Solow (1957) calculated that about four-fifths of the growth in US output per worker came from technical progress.

Ecological economics places his strongly neoclassical position, with Martin Weitzman's, at one end of a continuum of views on weak versus strong sustainability. Georgescu-Roegen and Daly stand at the other. Solow also criticised the Club of Rome's Limits to Growth as having 'simplistic' scenarios.

nature-eecon-257.title: Marginal rate of technical substitution
nature-eecon-257.text: The marginal rate of technical substitution is the amount by which one input must be reduced when one more unit of another is used so that output stays constant. Along an isoquant it shows the rate at which one input, such as capital or labour, can replace another. It equals the ratio of the two inputs' marginal products, and is the absolute value of the slope of the isoquant at the point in question. Isoquants slope downward because of diminishing marginal rates of technical substitution. When input proportions are cost-minimising, it equals the relative unit costs of the inputs, so the isoquant slope equals the isocost slope.

nature-eecon-252.title: Economic inequality: who gets how much, and why
nature-eecon-252.text:
Economic inequality is an umbrella term for income inequality, wealth inequality and consumption inequality, measurable between or within nations and sub-populations. The Gini coefficient is a widely used metric, where 0 reflects perfect equality. The Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index is a composite alternative.

Proposed drivers include imperfect labor markets, tax progressivity, unequal access to education, decline of unions and deregulation, technology and automation, and globalization. Wealth concentration means new wealth flows to those already wealthy, and Stiglitz attributes it to rent-seeking and political power, not market forces. A 2019 PNAS study found global warming widens inequality between countries, with 25% of the gap between developed and developing worlds attributable to it.

Views differ on what causes it and whether it matters. Socialists blame private ownership of capital, meritocrats see a natural outcome of differing talent, the capabilities approach sees capability deprivation, and some argue inequality rewards skills and risk-taking. Sources disagree on whether current levels are a problem or a spur to growth, though most researchers who analyze inequality argue today's levels are problematic and deserve mitigation.

nature-eecon-253.title: Global North and Global South
nature-eecon-253.text:
Global North and Global South group countries by socioeconomic characteristics, roughly developed and developing or least developed. UNCTAD puts Northern America, Europe, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand in the North, and Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, most of Asia and most of Oceania in the South. The terms are not strictly geographical, since many Southern countries lie in the Northern Hemisphere. The Brandt Line, proposed by Willy Brandt in the 1980s, shows the divide at roughly 30 degrees North; it is now criticized as outdated but still used to show global inequalities.

Dependency theory explains the divide through colonial relations: ex-colonial economies stay oriented to external demand, and peripheral primary exporters rely on core economies for manufactures. That led structuralists to advocate import-substitution industrialization. Scholars disagree on whether the South is converging with the North or inequality is widening. As of 2015 all but about the bottom 60 Southern nations were thought to be gaining, though Hickel and Wade argue inequality has risen since globalization. The label was meant to be less hierarchical than Third World, but critics call it a vague blanket term.

nature-eecon-250.title: Demographic transition: from high birth rates to low
nature-eecon-250.text:
China's birth rate fell from 6.6 births per woman before 1970 to 2.2 in 1980, at a pace no other population had matched. The demographic transition is the historical shift from high to low birth and death rates as societies gain technology, education (especially for women) and economic development.

The model has stages. In Stage 1, pre-industrial, birth and death rates are both high and roughly balanced, with death rates often above 40 per 1000 per year. In Stage 2 death rates fall and population grows. In Stage 3 birth rates diminish through better economic conditions, women's status and education, and access to contraception. In Stage 4 both rates are low and total population is stable. A proposed Stage 5 has sub-replacement fertility, below 2.1-2.2 children per woman.

The shift supports economic growth by reducing dilution of capital and land, raising investment in human capital, and enlarging the labor force relative to total population. But the model is only a model. It cannot predict the future, ignores migration and may not apply at very high levels of development, though some transition is widely accepted.

nature-eecon-255.title: Universal basic income: cash for everyone, no strings
nature-eecon-255.text:
Universal basic income is a welfare proposal in which all members of a population regularly receive a minimum income as an unconditional transfer, with no means test or work requirement. A full one meets basic needs; a lower one is partial. As of 2026 no country has a full UBI, while Mongolia (2010-2012) and Iran have had partial ones. A guaranteed minimum income, by contrast, goes only to those whose income is not enough to live on. Milton Friedman's negative income tax (1962) effectively sanctions a basic income.

Automation is a central rationale: if robotisation causes technological unemployment, a basic income would let everyone share a society's wealth. Links to growth are mixed. Proponents say it could raise growth by funding skills and risk-taking, while the degrowth movement also discusses it as part of arguing against growth. The Alaska Permanent Fund pays residents a yearly dividend from oil and gas revenues, resembling a sovereign wealth fund that invests resource income for future generations.

Economists and moral philosophers disagree over its cost, work incentives, inflation effects and fairness. A common argument against is upward pressure on prices, especially labor and housing rents. Critics also expect less work, and 1970 US negative income tax experiments saw a five percent decline in hours worked. A systematic review of unconditional cash transfers in low- and middle-income countries found possible gains in food security, school attendance and health-care spending.
